name: Multiculturalism
summary: Multiculturalism holds that a state should recognise and accommodate its cultural, ethnic, linguistic and religious diversity rather than require minorities to assimilate. It combines equal citizenship with group-sensitive measures such as language support, religious accommodation and, for national minorities and indigenous peoples, self-government. Critics argue it undermines cohesion, national identity or gender equality; adherents dispute this.

scope: Multiculturalism as a normative public philosophy and policy in Western liberal democracies, as the Stanford and Internet Encyclopedias of Philosophy define it (rejecting assimilation and defending group-differentiated rights, from Taylor, Kymlicka and Parekh) and as the Canadian Multiculturalism Act enacts it. It excludes the merely descriptive sense of demographic diversity, and the sources say little on economic questions.

keyFigures.role: Liberal theorist of group-differentiated minority rights
keyFigures.quote: Will Kymlicka has developed the most influential liberal theory of multiculturalism

keyFigures.role: Philosopher of the politics of recognition
keyFigures.quote: Some of the philosophers who defend a multicultural citizenship are Taylor, Kymlicka and Shachar.

keyFigures.role: Theorist of intercultural dialogue and multicultural justice
keyFigures.quote: Bhikhu Parekh contends that liberal theory cannot provide an impartial framework
